Let \(P=M\cap(0,\infty)\) and \(N=M\cap(-\infty,0)\).

First, a finite set of positive numbers with the same property has at most \(3\) elements. Indeed, if it had four positive elements \(p_1<p_2<p_3<p_4\), take the four largest. For the triple \(\{p_1,p_3,p_4\}\), the sums \(p_1+p_4\) and \(p_3+p_4\) exceed \(p_4\), so we must have \(p_1+p_3=p_4\). For the triple \(\{p_2,p_3,p_4\}\), similarly \(p_2+p_3=p_4\). Hence \(p_1=p_2\), contradiction.

Thus \(|P|\le 3\). For the negative elements, consider \(A=\{-x:x\in N\}\). If \(-a,-b,-c\in N\), then some sum \(-(a+b),-(a+c),-(b+c)\) lies in \(M\), hence in \(N\), so \(a+b,a+c,\) or \(b+c\in A\). Therefore \(A\) also satisfies the positive-set lemma, so \(|N|=|A|\le 3\).

Therefore
\[
|M|=|P|+|N|+1_{\{0\in M\}}\le 3+3+1=7.
\]

The set
\[
M=\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}
\]
has \(7\) elements and satisfies the property: triples containing \(0\) work using \(0+x=x\); all-positive triples work since \(1+2=3\); all-negative triples work since \(-2+(-1)=-3\); mixed triples without \(0\) have a suitable sum in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\subset M\).

Thus the maximum number of elements is \(\boxed{7}\).
